# `silk/crypto/aes`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Encrypt data with the AES block cipher (FIPS 197) in ECB, CBC, CTR, CFB, or OFB mode (NIST SP
800-38A).

## When to use
Use this module when a protocol or file format names AES-CBC, AES-CTR, AES-ECB, AES-CFB, or
AES-OFB, or when it needs the raw AES block function. These modes do not detect changes to the
ciphertext. To encrypt new data, prefer `silk.crypto.aes_gcm` or
`silk.crypto.chacha20_poly1305`, which also authenticate it.

## Details
[`Aes`](#Aes) holds an expanded 16-byte (AES-128), 24-byte (AES-192), or 32-byte (AES-256) key and
encrypts or decrypts one 16-byte block. [`AesCbc`](#AesCbc) and [`AesEcb`](#AesEcb) encrypt a message that
arrives in parts: call `update` for each part and `finish` at the end. With padding on, they add
and remove PKCS #7 padding, as OpenSSL does. [`AesCtr`](#AesCtr) XORs a key stream into the data, so the
same call encrypts and decrypts. The counter is the whole 16-byte block, incremented as one
big-endian number. [`AesCfb`](#AesCfb), [`AesCfb8`](#AesCfb8), and [`AesCfb1`](#AesCfb1) are cipher feedback with 128, 8, and
1-bit segments, and [`AesOfb`](#AesOfb) is output feedback. Nothing allocates.

The other AES modes have their own modules: `silk.crypto.aes_gcm`, `silk.crypto.aes_ccm`, and
`silk.crypto.aes_ocb` authenticate, `silk.crypto.aes_xts` encrypts storage sectors, and
`silk.crypto.aes_wrap` wraps keys.

When the build targets x86-64 or AArch64 with the `aes` CPU feature, each round is one AES
instruction. Otherwise the rounds use portable code that computes the S-box instead of reading a
table, so the time does not depend on the key or the data on any target.

## Errors
The functions return an [`AesError`](#AesError). Every check comes before the first write, and on an error
the output buffers do not change.

## Gotchas
CBC and CTR need a new IV for each message under the same key. With CTR, the same key and IV
used twice give away the XOR of the two plaintexts. ECB encrypts equal blocks to equal blocks,
so it shows patterns in the data. A wrong padding error from CBC decryption can act as an
oracle that lets an attacker decrypt the message, so authenticate the ciphertext before you
decrypt it. The values do not erase their copies of the key.

## Examples
### Encrypt and decrypt with AES-128-CBC
```silk
import silk.crypto.aes { AesCbc, AesError }
import silk.core.result { Result }

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let key: [u8; 16] = [0; 16]
  let iv: [u8; 16] = [0; 16]
  let mut encryptor = match AesCbc.encryptor(&key, &iv, true) {
    Result<AesCbc, AesError>.Success { value } => move value
    Result<AesCbc, AesError>.Failure { error: _ } => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  // Five bytes of plaintext become one padded block of ciphertext.
  let mut ciphertext: [u8; 16] = [0; 16]
  let mut written: usize = 0
  if let Result.Success { value } = encryptor.update(b"hello", &mut ciphertext) {
    written = value
  }
  if let Result.Success { value } = encryptor.finish(&mut ciphertext) {
    written = written + value
  }
  if written != 16 {
    return 1
  }
  let mut decryptor = match AesCbc.decryptor(&key, &iv, true) {
    Result<AesCbc, AesError>.Success { value } => move value
    Result<AesCbc, AesError>.Failure { error: _ } => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  let mut plaintext: [u8; 16] = [0; 16]
  if let Result.Success { value } = decryptor.update(&ciphertext, &mut plaintext) {
    if value != 0 {
      return 1
    }
  }
  return match decryptor.finish(&mut plaintext) {
    Result<usize, AesError>.Success { value } => {
      if value != 5 || plaintext[0] != 104 {
        return 1
      }
      return 0
    }
    Result<usize, AesError>.Failure { error: _ } => 1
  }
}
```

### Encrypt with AES-256-CTR
```silk
import silk.crypto.aes { AesCtr, AesError }
import silk.core.result { Result }

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let key: [u8; 32] = [1; 32]
  let iv: [u8; 16] = [0; 16]
  let mut stream = match AesCtr.make(&key, &iv) {
    Result<AesCtr, AesError>.Success { value } => move value
    Result<AesCtr, AesError>.Failure { error: _ } => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  let mut ciphertext: [u8; 5] = [0; 5]
  if let Result.Failure { error: _ } = stream.apply(b"hello", &mut ciphertext) {
    return 1
  }
  // A new stream with the same key and IV decrypts.
  let mut again = match AesCtr.make(&key, &iv) {
    Result<AesCtr, AesError>.Success { value } => move value
    Result<AesCtr, AesError>.Failure { error: _ } => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  let mut plaintext: [u8; 5] = [0; 5]
  if let Result.Failure { error: _ } = again.apply(&ciphertext, &mut plaintext) {
    return 1
  }
  if plaintext[0] != 104 || plaintext[4] != 111 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

<a id="Aes"></a>

## `Aes`

```silk
pub struct Aes
```

An expanded AES key (FIPS 197) that encrypts and decrypts single 16-byte blocks.

### When to use

Use it to build a block cipher mode that this module does not offer. For CBC, CTR, or ECB, use
[`AesCbc`](#AesCbc), [`AesCtr`](#AesCtr), or [`AesEcb`](#AesEcb). For new designs, use `silk.crypto.aes_gcm`.

### Details

[`Aes.make`](#Aes.impl.make) takes a 16-byte (AES-128), 24-byte (AES-192), or 32-byte (AES-256) key and expands
the encryption and decryption round keys once. The value is fixed-size and does not allocate.
With the `aes` CPU feature on x86-64 or AArch64, each round is one instruction. Otherwise the
portable rounds compute the S-box instead of reading a table, so the time does not depend on the
key or the data.

### Gotchas

Encrypting blocks one by one with the same key is ECB mode, which shows equal blocks. The value
holds key material and is not erased when it is dropped.

<a id="AesCbc"></a>

## `AesCbc`

```silk
pub struct AesCbc
```

A streaming AES-CBC encryptor or decryptor (NIST SP 800-38A), with or without PKCS #7 padding.

### When to use

Use it when a protocol or file format names AES-CBC, such as `aes-256-cbc` in OpenSSL or
Node.js. CBC does not detect changes to the ciphertext. For new designs, use
`silk.crypto.aes_gcm`.

### Details

Make one with [`AesCbc.encryptor`](#AesCbc.impl.encryptor) or [`AesCbc.decryptor`](#AesCbc.impl.decryptor), call [`AesCbc.update`](#AesCbc.impl.update) for each part
of the input, then [`AesCbc.finish`](#AesCbc.impl.finish). `update` writes whole blocks and keeps the rest, so the
output of all calls together does not depend on how the input was split. With padding on, a
decryptor keeps the last whole block until `finish`, which checks and removes the padding. The
key is 16, 24, or 32 bytes and the IV is 16 bytes. Nothing allocates.

### Gotchas

Use a new random IV for each message under the same key. A wrong padding error can act as an
oracle that decrypts the message for an attacker, so authenticate the ciphertext first. The
value holds key material and is not erased when it is dropped.

<a id="AesCbc.impl.update"></a>

### Method `update`

```silk
pub fn update(self: &mut Self, input: &[u8], output: &mut [u8]) -> Result<usize, AesError>
```

Encrypts or decrypts the whole blocks of the kept bytes plus `input` into `output`, keeps the
rest, and returns the number of bytes written.

The count is [`AesCbc.updateLength`](#AesCbc.impl.updateLength) of `input.length`, a multiple of 16. The bytes of
`output` after it do not change. `input` and `output` must not overlap.

#### Errors

- `OutputTooSmall` if `output` is shorter than [`AesCbc.updateLength`](#AesCbc.impl.updateLength). The state does not
  change.

<a id="AesCbc.impl.finish"></a>

### Method `finish`

```silk
pub fn finish(self: Self, output: &mut [u8]) -> Result<usize, AesError>
```

Ends the message, writes the last bytes to `output`, returns their number, and consumes the
state.

An encryptor with padding writes one 16-byte block. A decryptor with padding writes 0 to 15
bytes, the last block without its padding. Without padding, it writes nothing.

#### Errors

- `InvalidInputLength` without padding if the message is not a whole number of blocks, or for
  a decryptor with padding if the ciphertext is not a whole number of blocks.
- `InvalidPadding` for a decryptor with padding if the last block does not end in valid
  PKCS #7 padding.
- `OutputTooSmall` if `output` is shorter than the bytes to write.

Use it only when a protocol or file format requires AES-ECB, such as `aes-128-ecb` in OpenSSL or
Node.js. ECB encrypts equal blocks to equal blocks, so it shows patterns in the data. For new
designs, use `silk.crypto.aes_gcm`.

padding on, a decryptor keeps the last whole block until `finish`, which checks and removes the
padding. The key is 16, 24, or 32 bytes. There is no IV. Nothing allocates.

### Gotchas

The value holds key material and is not erased when it is dropped.

<a id="AesCtr"></a>

## `AesCtr`

```silk
pub struct AesCtr
```

A streaming AES-CTR key stream (NIST SP 800-38A) that encrypts and decrypts.

### When to use

Use it when a protocol or file format names AES-CTR, such as `aes-128-ctr` in OpenSSL or
Node.js. CTR does not detect changes to the ciphertext. For new designs, use
`silk.crypto.aes_gcm`.

### Details

The 16-byte IV is the first counter block. Each block of key stream is the encryption of the
counter, which then grows by one as a 128-bit big-endian number and wraps to zero after all
ones, as OpenSSL does. [`AesCtr.apply`](#AesCtr.impl.apply) XORs the key stream into the data, so the same call
encrypts and decrypts, and the result does not depend on how the data is split. Nothing
allocates.

### Gotchas

The same key and IV must never encrypt two messages. If they do, the XOR of the two ciphertexts
is the XOR of the two plaintexts. The value holds key material and is not erased when it is
dropped.

`output` must not overlap.

#### Errors

- `OutputTooSmall` if `output` is shorter than `input`. The state does not change.

## `AesCfb`

```silk
pub struct AesCfb
```

AES in full-block cipher feedback mode, CFB-128 (NIST SP 800-38A section 6.3).

### When to use

Use it where a protocol names AES-CFB, such as Node's `aes-256-cfb`. It does not detect changes
to the ciphertext. For new designs, use `silk.crypto.aes_gcm`.

### Details

The 16-byte IV is the first input block. Each key stream block is the encryption of the
previous 16 ciphertext bytes, so encryption and decryption differ: make the value with
[`AesCfb.encryptor`](#AesCfb.impl.encryptor) or [`AesCfb.decryptor`](#AesCfb.impl.decryptor). [`AesCfb.apply`](#AesCfb.impl.apply) takes the data in any split and
gives the same result. Nothing allocates.

### Gotchas

The same key and IV must never encrypt two messages. The value holds key material and is not
erased when it is dropped.

## `AesCfb8`

```silk
pub struct AesCfb8
```

AES in 8-bit cipher feedback mode, CFB-8 (NIST SP 800-38A section 6.3).

### When to use

Use it where a protocol names AES-CFB8, such as Node's `aes-128-cfb8`. It does not detect
changes to the ciphertext, and it runs one block encryption per byte.

### Details

The 16-byte IV is the first shift register. For each byte, the first byte of the encrypted
register is the key stream byte, and the register shifts left by one byte and takes the
ciphertext byte. Make the value with [`AesCfb8.encryptor`](#AesCfb8.impl.encryptor) or [`AesCfb8.decryptor`](#AesCfb8.impl.decryptor). Nothing
allocates.

### Gotchas

The same key and IV must never encrypt two messages. The value holds key material and is not
erased when it is dropped.

<a id="AesCfb1"></a>

## `AesCfb1`

```silk
pub struct AesCfb1
```

AES in 1-bit cipher feedback mode, CFB-1 (NIST SP 800-38A section 6.3).

### When to use

Use it where a protocol names AES-CFB1, such as Node's `aes-128-cfb1`. It does not detect
changes to the ciphertext, and it runs one block encryption per bit, so it is slow.

### Details

The 16-byte IV is the first shift register. Each byte is taken as eight bits, most significant
first, as OpenSSL does for byte input. For each bit, the top bit of the encrypted register is
the key stream bit, and the register shifts left by one bit and takes the ciphertext bit. Make
the value with [`AesCfb1.encryptor`](#AesCfb1.impl.encryptor) or [`AesCfb1.decryptor`](#AesCfb1.impl.decryptor). Nothing allocates.

### Gotchas

The same key and IV must never encrypt two messages. The value holds key material and is not
erased when it is dropped.

<a id="AesCfb1.impl"></a>

## Implementation `AesCfb1`

```silk
impl AesCfb1
```


Encrypts or decrypts `input` into the first `input.length` bytes of `output`.

The bytes of `output` after them do not change. `input` and `output` must not overlap.

<a id="AesOfb"></a>

## `AesOfb`

```silk
pub struct AesOfb
```

AES in output feedback mode, OFB (NIST SP 800-38A section 6.4).

### When to use

Use it where a protocol names AES-OFB, such as Node's `aes-256-ofb`. It does not detect changes
to the ciphertext. For new designs, use `silk.crypto.aes_gcm`.

### Details

The 16-byte IV is encrypted again and again to give the key stream, so it does not depend on the
data and [`AesOfb.apply`](#AesOfb.impl.apply) both encrypts and decrypts. The result does not depend on how the data
is split. Nothing allocates.

### Gotchas

The same key and IV must never encrypt two messages. If they do, the XOR of the two ciphertexts
is the XOR of the two plaintexts. The value holds key material and is not erased when it is
dropped.
